In my class project last semester our chatbot kept giving long, off-topic replies. My task was to make the answers short and consistent. I wrote five versions of the prompt, added a role, a fixed output format and two examples, and tested each version on 20 sample questions. I tracked how many answers followed the format, and it went from 8 out of 20 to 18 out of 20. After that I documented the final prompt so my teammates could reuse it.
I would make it better by adding more detail and trying again until it works.

I was asked to build a Zapier workflow for a small client during my freelance work, and I had never used webhooks before. I needed to deliver in one week. I read the documentation, built a small test zap on my own account, and asked one question in a community forum. I then built the real workflow in two days and wrote a one-page guide for the client. The client now uses it every day and saves about 3 hours a week.

I would build a test set of around 30 realistic inputs and run both prompts on the same set with the same settings. For example, for a classification task I compare accuracy against a baseline of correct labels. For open-ended tasks I use a rubric with scores for relevance, accuracy and clarity, and I check a sample by hand because automatic scores can be wrong. I would pick prompt B only if it wins on the main metric and does not break any case that prompt A handled correctly.
